title: How people really talk ({euh}, {ben}, {hein}, {quoi}, {en fait}, {du coup}, {genre}, {bref})
description: The small words French speakers use to think aloud and react, the short forms of fast speech, and when each one fits.
can_do: Fill a pause, start an answer or react with {euh}, {ben}, {bon}, {ouais} or {bof}
Understand fast speech: {je sais pas}, {t'as}, {y'a}, {chais pas}
Pick the short or the full form for a friend, a boss or a note
line: With friends, French speakers fill their speech with small words and short forms; in writing and with people they say {vous} to, they keep the full forms.

parts.heading: Thinking aloud: {euh}, {ben}, {bah}
text: {euh} fills a pause, as um does in English. {ben} and {bah} start an answer that needs a second's thought, like well. {bah oui} and {ben non} mean well, yes and well, no: the answer is obvious.

lines: Euh… on va où, d'abord ?
Um… where are we going first?
Ben, à la boulangerie.
Well, to the bakery.
Tu viens samedi ? Bah oui !
Are you coming on Saturday? Well, yes!

parts.heading: Starting and closing: {bon}, {alors}, {voilà}, {enfin}, {bref}
text: {bon} and {alors} open a new step, like right or so. {voilà} closes one: there you go. {enfin} corrects what you just said: well, I mean. {bref} cuts a long story short: anyway.

lines: Bon, je te présente Maya.
Right, this is Maya.
Alors, à gauche, c'est la bibliothèque.
So, on the left, that's the library.
Et voilà, c'est mon quartier.
And there you go, that's my neighbourhood.
Noé est grand, enfin, plus grand que l'année dernière.
Noé is tall, well, taller than last year.
Le marché, la piscine, la boulangerie… Bref, il y a tout ici.
The market, the pool, the bakery… Anyway, there's everything here.
Bon, au revoir, madame !
Right, goodbye!

parts.heading: Checking the listener follows: {hein}, {tu vois}, {quoi}
text: {hein} at the end of a sentence asks the listener to agree: right? {tu vois} means you see. {quoi} at the end of a sentence rounds the thought off, like you know or that's all.
parts.note: Alone, {Hein ?} means what?: blunt between friends, rude to someone you say {vous} to. With them, say {Pardon ?}

lines: Il fait humide aujourd'hui, hein ?
It's damp today, isn't it?
C'est Hugo, le pote dont je t'ai parlé, tu vois ?
That's Hugo, the mate I told you about, you see?
Il chante mal et fort, mais il adore ça, quoi.
He sings badly and loudly, but he loves it, you know.

parts.heading: Explaining: {en fait}, {du coup}
text: {en fait} means actually: it brings in what is really true. {du coup} means so: it gives the result of what came before. Some speakers put {du coup} in almost every sentence.

lines: En fait, la piscine ferme à huit heures.
Actually, the pool closes at eight.
En fait, j'ai oublié ma clé chez Léa.
Actually, I left my key at Léa's.
Je déteste danser, en fait.
I hate dancing, actually.
Maya a rien dit. Du coup, je sais pas si elle vient.
Maya didn't say anything. So I don't know if she's coming.
La météo dit qu'il va pleuvoir. Du coup, on va à la bibliothèque.
The forecast says it's going to rain. So we're going to the library.

parts.heading: Reacting: {ouais}, {bof}, {franchement}, {genre}
text: {ouais} is yeah. {bof} is meh: not really, not great. {franchement} means honestly and comes before a real opinion. {genre} means like: it makes a number rough or brings in an example.

lines: On prend les vélos ? Ouais !
Shall we take the bikes? Yeah!
Tu aimes la piscine ? Bof.
Do you like the pool? Meh.
Franchement, tu danses trop bien !
Honestly, you dance really well!
Il y a, genre, dix boulangeries.
There are, like, ten bakeries.

parts.heading: Short forms of fast speech
text: In fast speech most people drop {ne} and keep {pas}. They say {on} for {nous}. {tu} loses its u before a vowel: {t'as}, {t'es}. {il y a} sounds like {y'a}, and {je ne sais pas} sounds like {chais pas}.
Almost everyone uses these forms every day. You need to understand them; the full forms are always right to say.

rows.fr: En hiver, y'a personne à la piscine.
rows.en: In winter, there's nobody at the pool.

rows.fr: En hiver, il n'y a personne à la piscine.

parts.heading: When each form fits
text: With friends and family, use the small words freely. With a stranger, a teacher or a boss, {euh}, {bon}, {alors}, {en fait}, {enfin}, {du coup}, {bref} and {franchement} are still fine in speech, but say {oui} for {ouais}, and leave out {ben}, {bah}, {bof}, {genre}, {hein} and {quoi}.
In writing, keep {ne} and the full forms. In a text message to a friend, people often write {je sais pas} and {t'as} too.

cmp.right: With a stranger or a boss

checks.ask: Hugo asks if you liked the film. It was not great. Which answer fits?
checks.why: {bof} says not really, not great. Hugo is a friend, so it fits.

checks.ask: Léa writes a note to Mme Garnier. Which sentence fits the note?

options.text: Chais pas si Noé est chez vous.
Je sais pas si Noé est chez vous.
Je ne sais pas si Noé est chez vous.

checks.why: A note is writing, and Léa says {vous} to Mme Garnier, so {ne} stays: {Je ne sais pas}.
{t'as} is {tu as} said fast, so {T'as faim ?} is {Tu as faim ?}: are you hungry?
